notes.meaning: Jesus learned that the Pharisees were closely tracking His growing popularity and the large crowds coming to Him. Because His time to suffer had not yet come, He chose not to trigger an early conflict with the religious leaders in Jerusalem. He quietly stepped away so He could carry out His mission in peace.

John clarifies that Jesus let His disciples perform the water baptisms rather than doing them Himself. Jesus reserved His energy for preaching the good news, which was His primary work. This also kept people from boasting that they were better than others because Jesus personally baptized them.

differ.view: Reformed Christians teach that baptism does not depend on the person who administers it, but carries Christ's full authority and blessing regardless of who performs the washing.
Baptists note that Jesus leaving baptism to others shows water baptism does not save the soul, but serves as an outward act of obedience and public testimony.

notes.meaning: Jesus left the region of Judea and headed north back to Galilee. He moved away from Jerusalem because the ruling religious council held less direct power in Galilee. This move allowed Him to continue teaching and training His followers safely.

The most direct road from Judea to Galilee went right through the district of Samaria. Many strict Jews took a longer route around the region to avoid the Samaritans completely. Jesus chose the direct path because God had a divine appointment waiting for Him there.

Jesus arrived at a Samaritan town named Sychar, near ancient Shechem. This town was located right next to the parcel of land Jacob had purchased and later gave to Joseph. It was a place rich with Old Testament memories for the people living there.

Jacob's well was located there, and Jesus sat down beside it because He was exhausted from walking. It was around noon, the hottest part of the day, and He had traveled on foot without resting. His deep weariness shows that He was truly human and felt the full weight of physical fatigue.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think John counts hours the Roman way, so the "sixth hour" would be about 6 in the evening. That was a usual time for drawing water.

notes.meaning: A Samaritan woman arrived at the well to draw water in the heat of midday. Women normally came together in the cool morning or evening, so her arrival alone shows she was likely an outcast. Jesus looked past social walls and kindly asked her for a drink of water.

The disciples were not with Jesus because they had walked into the nearby town to buy food. This left Jesus by Himself at the well with no rope or bucket to draw water. It also shows that Jews were willing to buy groceries from Samaritans even while avoiding close friendship with them.

The woman was shocked that a Jewish man would ask her for a drink. Jews and Samaritans had despised each other for generations, and strict Jews would never share a drinking cup with a Samaritan. She could immediately tell He was Jewish from His clothing and dialect.

Jesus told her that if she understood God's generosity and knew who was speaking, she would have asked Him for living water. While running spring water was commonly called living water, Jesus was speaking of the Holy Spirit and the free gift of eternal life. He used her everyday chore to invite her into saving truth.

The woman pointed out that Jesus had no bucket or rope, and the well was very deep. She took His words in a purely physical sense and could not see how He could reach any fresh water. Jacob's well was cut deep into solid rock, making it impossible to draw water without tools.

She asked Jesus if He thought He was greater than the patriarch Jacob, who had dug the well for his own family and herds. The Samaritans took deep pride in claiming Jacob as their forefather. She doubted that this tired traveler could produce better water than the great founder of their traditions.

Jesus answered that anyone who drinks ordinary well water will always get thirsty again. Physical water can refresh the body for only a few hours before the thirst returns. Earthly comforts and pleasures can never fully satisfy the deepest desires of the human heart.

Jesus promised that whoever drinks the water He provides will never be spiritually thirsty again. His gift of grace and the Holy Spirit becomes an active fountain inside the believer, bubbling up into eternal life. This divine life continually refreshes the soul from the inside out.

The woman asked Jesus to give her this water so she would never be thirsty or have to haul heavy water jars to the well again. She still missed the spiritual meaning and thought only of saving herself physical labor. Even though she did not understand, she was beginning to trust Him enough to ask for His help.

Jesus told her to go call her husband and return to the well. He shifted the conversation to awaken her conscience and show her the hidden sins in her life. Before she could welcome the gift of living water, she had to see her need for God's forgiveness.

The woman replied that she had no husband, trying to keep her messy personal life hidden. Jesus commended her for speaking truthfully, while preparing to reveal that He already knew her entire story. His gentle answer showed both absolute kindness and complete insight into her heart.

Jesus told her that she had been married to five different men in the past, and the man she currently lived with was not her husband. By uncovering her secret past, Jesus proved that He possessed supernatural knowledge from God. He exposed her guilt not to crush her, but to lead her to repentance.

The woman told Jesus she could see He was a prophet sent by God. Her earlier teasing tone disappeared completely once she realized a complete stranger knew the secrets of her life. She recognized that He was speaking with genuine divine authority.

She raised the ancient debate between Jews and Samaritans over whether people should worship on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem. She may have been trying to steer the conversation away from her sins, or genuinely seeking answers from a real prophet. Mount Gerizim stood right next to them as the historic center of Samaritan religion.

Jesus told her that an hour was coming when true worship would not depend on Mount Gerizim or Jerusalem. The old system of ritual worship tied to one special location was coming to an end. Under the new covenant, believers from every nation can approach God anywhere as their loving Father.

Jesus made it clear that the Samaritans worshiped in ignorance because they rejected the Old Testament prophets and mixed true faith with error. The Jews held the true revelation of God because God chose them to deliver His scriptures and bring forth the Messiah. Salvation reaches the whole world through the Jewish people.

Jesus announced that the time had already arrived for true worshipers to worship the Father in spirit and in truth. Acceptable worship does not depend on outward ceremonies, temple buildings, or animal sacrifices, but on a sincere heart led by the Holy Spirit. God Himself is actively looking for people who will worship Him this way.

Jesus explained that God is Spirit, so those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth. God does not have a physical body and cannot be trapped inside a single building or mountain shrine. Because of who God is, our worship must be genuine, spiritual, and aligned with His revealed truth.

The woman said she knew the Messiah was coming and would explain all things to them when He arrived. Even with their limited scriptures, the Samaritans waited for the great Prophet promised through Moses to bring complete understanding. She looked forward to the day when the Messiah would resolve all religious disputes.

Jesus revealed His true identity plainly by telling her, 'I who speak to you am He.' While He kept this title hidden in Judea to prevent political riots, He shared it openly with an outcast Samaritan woman. His clear answer answered her deepest questions and offered her salvation.

The disciples came back from town and were astonished to see Jesus talking publicly with a woman. Cultural traditions of the rabbis strongly discouraged men from speaking to women in public, especially Samaritan women. Even though they were puzzled, the disciples reverently kept quiet because they trusted their Master.
